reference.source: GeneReviews / Smith's Recognizable Patterns of Human Malformation
clinicalPearls: Caused by loss of the paternally expressed 14q32 genes, through maternal uniparental disomy 14, a paternal 14q32 deletion, or an imprinting defect
Pre- and postnatal growth restriction with short stature and small hands and feet is typical
Neonatal hypotonia and feeding difficulty overlap strongly with Prader-Willi syndrome in infancy
Precocious or early puberty is characteristic and a useful distinguishing clue
Truncal obesity and increased weight tend to develop in later childhood
Motor delay is usually mild and intellectual disability mild or absent, while a triangular face and frontal bossing may resemble Silver-Russell syndrome
It is often under-diagnosed because it overlaps phenotypically with both Prader-Willi and Silver-Russell syndromes
reference.pathophysiology: Temple syndrome is an imprinting disorder caused by absent expression of the paternally expressed genes at the imprinted 14q32 locus, such as DLK1 and RTL1, with relative excess of the maternally expressed gene MEG3. This most commonly results from maternal uniparental disomy 14, but the identical picture follows a paternal deletion of 14q32 or a primary imprinting (methylation) defect. Disturbed dosage of these growth- and metabolism-related imprinted genes produces the growth restriction, hypotonia, early puberty, and later obesity.
additionalDifferentials: Prader-Willi syndrome, the major infancy mimic
Silver-Russell syndrome, given growth restriction and a triangular face
Kagami-Ogata syndrome, the reciprocal paternal-UPD14 disorder
additionalInvestigations: Methylation analysis of the 14q32 (MEG3/DLK1) differentially methylated region as the first-line test
Microsatellite or SNP analysis to confirm maternal uniparental disomy 14 and distinguish it from deletion or epimutation
Karyotype to detect a Robertsonian translocation involving chromosome 14
Chromosomal microarray, usually normal but useful to exclude deletions and duplications
Growth monitoring and endocrine or pubertal assessment, including bone age
redFlags: Severe neonatal hypotonia with feeding failure
Rapid weight gain with obesity-related complications
reference.prognosis: Generally favourable, with usually mild or no intellectual disability; the main issues are early puberty, short stature, and a tendency to obesity, all of which respond to appropriate endocrine and dietary management.
pitfalls: Missing the diagnosis because it mimics Prader-Willi and Silver-Russell syndromes
Relying on karyotype or microarray, which miss uniparental disomy and imprinting defects
Overlooking precocious puberty as a distinguishing feature
Failing to test for uniparental disomy 14 when a chromosome 14 Robertsonian translocation is present
references: Smith's Recognizable Patterns of Human Malformation
Cassidy and Allanson's Management of Genetic Syndromes
management: Support neonatal feeding difficulty and hypotonia with assisted or nasogastric feeding and early physiotherapy until oromotor function improves
Monitor growth closely and consider growth hormone therapy for the associated short stature under endocrine supervision
Treat precocious or early puberty with a GnRH analogue to arrest premature pubertal progression and protect adult height
Institute early dietary and lifestyle measures to prevent the truncal obesity that emerges in later childhood
Provide developmental assessment with physiotherapy and educational support for motor delay
Coordinate multidisciplinary paediatric, endocrine and dietetic follow-up
Offer genetic counselling clarifying recurrence risk according to the underlying mechanism of uniparental disomy, deletion or imprinting defect, and test for a Robertsonian translocation
